title: Network waterfalls: request stages, preload hints and HTTP/2
description: The network panel shows why your page is slow, once you know how to read it. This quiz walks through the bars: what each segment of a request means, which requests block rendering, and when an "optimization" only moves the delay further down the list.

questions.title: Reading one request bar from left to right, which order of stages is correct?
questions.description: Not every request shows every stage. A cached response or a reused connection skips several. The stages that do appear always keep the same order.

images.alt: One request bar exploded into eight labeled segments: Queued, Stalled, DNS, Initial connection, TLS, Request sent, Waiting (TTFB), Content download
images.caption: The eight segments of a request bar. The rest of the quiz refers back to this figure.

options.text: Queued → Stalled → DNS → Initial connection → TLS → Request sent → Waiting (TTFB) → Content download
DNS → Queued → TLS → Initial connection → Request sent → Content download → Waiting (TTFB)
Stalled → Queued → Initial connection → DNS → TLS → Waiting (TTFB) → Request sent → Content download
Initial connection → TLS → DNS → Queued → Stalled → Request sent → Content download → Waiting (TTFB)

questions.explanation:
The bar follows the order in which things must happen before any data can move. First the browser waits until it's allowed to send the request (Queued, Stalled). Then it looks up the server's address (DNS) and opens a connection, with TLS on top if the connection is encrypted (Initial connection, TLS). It sends the request (Request sent), waits for the server to process it and reply (Waiting, or TTFB), and finally receives the body (Content download).

Chrome DevTools, Firefox and WebPageTest all draw the bar this way because it matches the real sequence of events. A request can skip stages in the middle. For example, a bar with no DNS or connection segments means the browser reused a connection it already had. The stages never appear out of order.

questions.title: One request has a long Stalled segment, and another has a long Waiting (TTFB) segment. What's the difference?

options.text: Stalled is a wait on the client: there's no free connection yet, or the browser is holding the request back on purpose. Waiting is the server's processing time plus one round trip. You fix the first on the client, and the second on the server or in its data access.
They mean the same thing. Different tools just use different labels for it.
Stalled always means a network outage, and Waiting always means a slow disk on the server.
Stalled happens after the response starts arriving, and Waiting happens before the request is sent.

questions.explanation:
Both segments look like idle time. They have different causes, so you look for the fix in different places.

Stalled happens before the request is sent. The browser wants to make the request but can't yet, usually because it's waiting for a free connection (a later question covers the HTTP/1.1 limit of six connections). Check the client and how many requests you make in parallel.

Waiting (TTFB) happens after the request is sent. The request is on its way, and the browser is waiting for the server to process it and send back the first byte. Check the server: application logic, cache state, and how far the server or edge node is from the user.

questions.title: style.css is a static file with no server-side logic, but its Waiting (TTFB) segment is long. What does that suggest?

options.text: The server or CDN is slow to respond even for static content. The edge cache might be cold, the request might have gone to a busy origin after a cache miss, or the file isn't served from the edge cache you expected.
Static files never have a Waiting segment, so DevTools must be drawing it wrong.
The server compresses the file at an unusually high level.
The browser deprioritizes static assets to save bandwidth for scripts.

questions.explanation: Every HTTP response has a TTFB: the server's processing time plus one round trip. Even for a static file, the server has to receive the request, find the file and start sending it, even if finding it takes a single disk read. A long TTFB on a static file usually means the request missed a fast cache. The edge node may not have the file yet, the request may have gone to a slower origin, or the CDN may not cache that file type the way you think. Compression changes the size of the response, which affects Content download. It doesn't change how long the server takes to start.

questions.title: A 12 KB JSON response has a long Content download segment. What are the two most likely causes?

options.text: The connection is slow or has high latency (throttling or a poor network path), or the response isn't compressed, so many more bytes travel over the network than 12 KB suggests.
The server took a long time to process the request before responding.
DNS resolution failed partway through and was retried.
A render-blocking script earlier on the page delayed the start of this request.

questions.explanation: Content download measures only transfer time: how long the bytes take to arrive after the server starts sending them. If a small file downloads slowly, either the connection is slow or unreliable, or the file is bigger in transit than its size suggests. The usual reason is missing gzip or Brotli compression, which can make JSON several times larger. Server processing time appears in Waiting. DNS failures appear as failed or retried DNS segments. A late start appears in Stalled or Queued.

questions.title: A request's bar starts at Waiting, with no Queued, DNS, Initial connection or TLS segments before it. What could explain that?

options.text: The browser reused an open keep-alive connection to the same origin, so it didn't need a DNS lookup or a new connection.
The request is a later stream on an HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 connection that an earlier request already opened.
The response came from the disk cache, so the browser never sent a request.
dns-prefetch resolved the hostname during idle time before the request was made.

questions.explanation: Missing connection setup almost always means the browser reused a connection. It already had a live connection to that origin, either an HTTP/1.1 keep-alive connection or an existing HTTP/2 connection, so it could send the request right away. A disk cache hit looks different. The browser never sends a request, so DevTools shows an almost instant entry labeled "(disk cache)" with no Waiting segment either. And `dns-prefetch` only removes the DNS segment. A request it helped would still show Initial connection and TLS.

questions.title: TTFB is the server's processing time plus how many network round trips?
questions.description: Assume a simple request over a connection that's already open, with no redirects, retries or packet loss.
questions.explanation: TTFB (Time to First Byte) includes one round trip. The request travels to the server, the server processes it, and the first byte of the response travels back. That's why distance matters so much. A server on the other side of the world adds real milliseconds to every request, however fast its code is. CDNs put edge servers near users to shorten that distance.

questions.title: How do a memory cache hit, a disk cache hit and a 304 Not Modified response usually differ in the waterfall?

options.text: A memory cache hit appears almost instantly with no network segments. A disk cache hit is also fast, but the browser reads the file from storage first. A 304 is a real request with a real Waiting segment. The server replies "unchanged" instead of sending the body again, so Content download is tiny or missing.
All three look the same, because none of them use the network.
A 304 is the fastest of the three, because the browser skips the round trip.
Reading from the disk cache always takes longer than downloading the file again.

questions.explanation: Each one does a different amount of work, so each one looks different. A memory cache hit comes straight from RAM with no network activity, and DevTools shows a plain entry without segments. A disk cache hit also skips the network but reads from storage, so it can be a little slower. A 304 Not Modified does use the network. The browser sends a conditional request with `If-None-Match` or `If-Modified-Since`, and if the resource hasn't changed, the server replies with a status and no body. So a 304 has a real Waiting (TTFB) segment, plus connection and TLS segments if no connection was open yet, and an almost empty Content download.

questions.title: In this waterfall, why doesn't icons.woff2 start downloading until both index.html and app.css have finished?

images.alt: Three request bars forming a staircase: index.html, then app.css starting after it finishes, then icons.woff2 starting after app.css finishes
images.caption: Each row starts only after the row above it reveals it.

options.text: The browser only finds a resource after it parses the file that references it. The font is loaded through an @import inside app.css, and the browser doesn't find app.css until it has parsed enough of index.html.
The browser throttles font requests to save bandwidth for more important assets.
The server has a strict request queue for each client and handles every asset one at a time.
The font file is too big for the connection's initial congestion window, so it waits for the next one.

questions.explanation: This shape is called a staircase: a chain of discoveries where each request starts only after the one above it reveals it. The browser has to parse the HTML before it knows `app.css` exists. Then it has to download and parse `app.css` before it sees the `@import` that points to the font. Nothing is throttled or queued on purpose. Each step had to wait because the browser didn't know about the next request yet. The fix is to shorten the chain: inline critical CSS, replace `@import` with a `<link>` in the HTML, or use `<link rel="preload">` so the browser learns about a deeply nested resource early.

questions.title: script7.js and script8.js stay Stalled for a long time before anything else happens. Why?

images.alt: Eight script requests over HTTP/1.1; the first six start immediately, script7 and script8 sit Stalled until a connection frees up
images.caption: All eight requests go to the same origin.

options.text: HTTP/1.1 limits how many connections a browser opens to one origin, six in most browsers. script7 and script8 wait until one of the first six finishes and frees a connection.
The server rate-limits those two files.
Those two files are larger and take longer to transfer.
The browser waits for the user to interact with the page before requesting them.

questions.explanation: This is the six-connection limit. Under HTTP/1.1, browsers limit how many connections they open to one origin, so the seventh and eighth requests wait until an earlier one finishes. The wait shows up as Stalled, not as a slow transfer. Once they start, those files can download in a normal amount of time. Two common HTTP/1.1 workarounds existed because of this limit. Domain sharding spread assets across extra subdomains to get more parallel connections, and bundling combined many small files into a few large ones.

questions.title: The same eight scripts load again, this time over HTTP/2. What changed?

images.alt: The same eight script requests over HTTP/2; only script1 pays for connection setup, the rest start almost immediately on the same connection
images.caption: Same eight files, same origin, one connection.

options.text: All eight requests share one connection, so only the first pays for DNS and connection setup. The others start as soon as that connection is ready, without waiting for a free slot.
HTTP/2 makes each file smaller, so downloads finish faster.
HTTP/2 removes the need for a TLS handshake.
Each request still opens its own connection, but now the connections open in parallel.

questions.explanation: This is multiplexing. HTTP/2 sends many independent streams over one connection, so the six-connection limit doesn't apply. The first request pays the one-time cost of DNS, the TCP handshake and TLS, and every later request uses the connection that's already open. Some things stay the same. The files are the same size, and TLS still happens. Multiplexing removes the limit on connections, but it doesn't add bandwidth, so eight streams on one connection still share the same bytes per second.

questions.title: hero.jpg is this page's LCP candidate, but its request starts long after index.html finishes downloading. What's the most likely cause?

images.alt: A waterfall where hero.jpg starts only after bundle.js has been downloading for a while, with an LCP marker line at the point hero.jpg finishes
images.caption: index.html and app.css finish early. bundle.js runs, and only then does hero.jpg start.

options.text: bundle.js runs first and adds the `` tag to the page. The preload scanner only reads the original HTML, so it had no image tag to find.
The image file is unusually large.
The server delays image responses on purpose to prioritize scripts.
The image is on a third-party CDN, and its DNS result can't be cached.

questions.explanation: The preload scanner reads ahead in the HTML to find resources to fetch early, but it only sees what's in the markup. When JavaScript adds an `` later, which component frameworks do all the time, the browser doesn't find the image until that script has run. Everything that depends on the image is delayed too, including LCP, because LCP is recorded only when the largest visible element paints. A large file or a slow host can make the download longer once it starts. Neither explains why it starts so late. This is a discovery problem.

questions.title: A page loads its only stylesheet with a plain `<link rel="stylesheet">` in `<head>`. Which changes would stop it from blocking rendering?

options.text: Add a media attribute that doesn't apply to the current page, such as media="print". The browser still downloads the file at low priority, but doesn't wait for it before the first paint.
Inline the styles needed for above-the-fold content in the HTML, and load the rest of the stylesheet in a way that doesn't block the first render.
Move the `<link>` tag to the end of `<body>`, just before the closing tag.
Add the defer attribute to the `<link>` tag, as you would on a `<script>`.

questions.explanation: The browser waits for render-blocking stylesheets before the first paint, because painting without them would show unstyled content. A media query that doesn't match avoids the block, because the browser only waits for stylesheets that apply right now. A print stylesheet downloads without delaying the page. Inlining critical CSS works for a different reason. The styles needed for the first paint are already in the HTML, so the browser doesn't wait for an external file. Moving the `<link>` to the end of `<body>` doesn't remove the block. The browser still fetches and applies it before painting the content after it, and now it finds the file later, which usually makes things worse. `defer` doesn't work on `<link rel="stylesheet">` at all. It only changes when a `<script>` runs.

questions.title: Three scripts load with different attributes. Which one pauses the HTML parser both while it downloads and while it runs?

options.text: a.js. A script with no attribute stops parsing while it downloads and while it runs.
b.js. An async script downloads while parsing continues and runs as soon as it's ready. It pauses the parser only while it runs.
c.js. A deferred script downloads while parsing continues and runs after parsing finishes.
All three block the parser in the same way, whatever their attributes.

questions.explanation: A plain `<script>` without `async` or `defer` blocks parsing the most. The browser stops, downloads the file, runs it, and only then continues with the document, because the script might call `document.write` or depend on running exactly where it is. An `async` script downloads in the background and pauses the parser only when it runs. It runs whenever it's ready, so you can't predict its order relative to other scripts. A `defer` script also downloads in the background, but it waits until parsing is done, and deferred scripts run in the order they appear in the document. That predictable order makes `defer` the safer choice for scripts that don't need to run right away.

questions.title: widget.js and app.js are about the same size, but widget.js has a much wider bar. What does the extra width show?

images.alt: Two request bars of similar total data: app.js on the same origin with only Waiting and Download, widget.js on a third-party origin with DNS, connection, TLS, Waiting, and Download
images.caption: app.js reuses an open connection. widget.js opens a new one.

options.text: widget.js comes from a new third-party origin (ads.example.com), so the browser has to look up DNS and open a new TCP and TLS connection before requesting the file. app.js uses a connection that's already open, so it skips these steps.
widget.js is compressed less efficiently than app.js.
widget.js is waiting behind other requests on the same connection.
The server that hosts widget.js has slower disks.

questions.explanation: This is the cost of connecting to a new third-party origin. The first time the browser contacts an origin, it needs a DNS lookup, a TCP handshake and, for HTTPS, a TLS handshake before any response data arrives. Requests to your own origin usually skip this, because an earlier request on the page already opened the connection. You pay this cost once per origin, however many requests you make and however big they are. A page with a dozen small third-party scripts from a dozen hostnames can spend more time on handshakes than on downloads. Using fewer origins, or hosting the files yourself, cuts that time.

questions.title: This request ends with a 200, but three small bars come before it. What are they, and what do they cost?

images.alt: Three small redirect request bars before a final, full request that actually downloads content
images.caption: GET /promo redirects twice before it reaches the real page.

options.text: Each one is a redirect response, such as a 301. Each costs a full round trip before the browser even knows the final URL, and none of them deliver any content.
They're automatic retries after failed connection attempts.
They're preconnects the browser made on its own.
They're the DNS, TCP and TLS segments of the final request, shown as separate rows.

questions.explanation: A redirect chain adds small, almost empty round trips before the request you actually wanted. Each redirect response has almost no body, only a status code and a `Location` header. The browser still sends the request, waits for the reply, and then starts again with the new URL. Three redirects mean three extra round trips before any useful content arrives. Fix the original link so it points straight to the final URL.

questions.title: Comparing block and swap in this font-loading timeline, which statements are true?

images.alt: Two timelines for the same font load: block shows invisible text until the web font is ready, swap shows a fallback font immediately that later swaps to the web font
images.caption: Same font file, same load time. Only what you see while it loads changes.

options.text: With block, text in that font stays invisible until the web font loads or a short timeout ends. This is FOIT (flash of invisible text).
With swap, a fallback font appears right away and is replaced by the web font when it loads. This is FOUT (flash of unstyled text).
Both strategies change how long the font file takes to download.
swap guarantees no layout shift when the fonts change.

questions.explanation: `font-display` has no effect on the network. The font file downloads at the same speed either way. It only decides what the browser shows while the text is ready but the web font hasn't arrived. `block` hides the text, which causes FOIT if the font is slow. `swap` shows a fallback font right away and switches later, which causes FOUT: the typeface changes while someone is reading. If the fallback font's letters are a different width from the web font's, that switch also causes layout shift. `size-adjust` and fallback fonts with matching metrics reduce the shift.

questions.title: A page's waterfall finishes in under a second, every request is fast and nothing is stalled. Yet the page still feels slow when you use it. What doesn't the waterfall show?

options.text: Time spent running JavaScript on the main thread after the network work is done. The network can be fast and idle while script execution and layout still block interaction.
The exact number of DNS lookups on the page.
Whether the connection used HTTP/2 or HTTP/3.
Whether the responses were compressed.

questions.explanation: A waterfall shows the network side: when data moved and how long it took. After the last response arrives, it has nothing more to show. The browser may still need to parse, compile and run a lot of JavaScript, and do style and layout work. All of that runs on the main thread and can delay the response to a click. If the waterfall is short and clean but the page feels slow, look at the main thread in the Performance panel or a JavaScript profiler.

questions.title: What's the practical difference between preconnect and dns-prefetch?

options.text: preconnect does the DNS lookup, the TCP handshake and, for HTTPS, the TLS handshake in advance. dns-prefetch only resolves the hostname to an IP address.
dns-prefetch does everything preconnect does, only faster.
preconnect only works over HTTP, and dns-prefetch only works over HTTPS.
They're two names for the same behavior.

questions.explanation: Both hints start connecting to an origin early, and they do different amounts of work. `dns-prefetch` is the cheaper one. It looks up the IP address ahead of time and saves one round trip. `preconnect` also opens the TCP connection and, for HTTPS, completes the TLS handshake, so when the real request comes, only the request and response are left. That extra work has a cost for each origin, so use `preconnect` only for origins you're sure the page will need soon. The next question looks at when that's worth it.

questions.title: When is preconnect worth adding?

images.alt: Bars showing what preconnect removes (DNS, connection, TLS) and what preload removes (late discovery) from a request's timeline
images.caption: preconnect shortens the start of the bar. preload makes the bar start earlier.

options.text: You're sure the page will use the origin very soon, like a font host or an API you call on load.
Without it, the connection would start cold right when it's needed, so opening it early saves measurable time.
You want to warm up every third-party origin on the page, in case any of them get used.
The browser already has an open connection to that origin from an earlier request.

questions.explanation: Use `preconnect` for specific origins. Each connection it opens uses a socket and some memory, and the setup time is wasted if nothing uses it. Browsers only honor a few preconnects and ignore the rest. It helps when you know the origin, know the page needs it soon, and know the connection would otherwise start cold at a bad moment. Preconnecting to many origins just in case backfires. The small early budget of connections and bandwidth gets split across origins that may never be used, leaving less for the ones that matter. And if a connection is already open, preconnect has nothing to do.

questions.title: Which resource hint fetches a resource at high priority without running or applying it?
questions.description: Answer with the value you'd put in `<link rel="...">`.
questions.explanation: `preload` tells the browser to fetch a resource now, at high priority, and nothing else. It doesn't run a script, apply a stylesheet or render an image. That's what makes it useful: the browser finds the resource earlier, and nothing changes about what happens when it arrives. Use it when the parser would otherwise find something too late, like a font behind an `@import` or an image that JavaScript adds.

questions.title: What is prefetch for, and at what priority does it run?

options.text: Fetching a resource the next page will probably need, before the user goes there, at idle or low priority so it doesn't slow down the current page.
Fetching the current page's most important resources at the highest priority.
Warming up a DNS, TCP and TLS connection to the origin the current page is already on.
Downloading a cached resource again so the cached copy doesn't go stale.

questions.explanation: `prefetch` is the only hint for a future page. It's a guess about where the user will go next. The user might never go there, so browsers fetch at low or idle priority and don't compete with the current page's resources. `preload` works the other way around. It's for something the current page needs right away.

questions.title: Why does a JavaScript module graph benefit from modulepreload more than from a single preload tag?

options.text: The browser doesn't know a module's imports until it parses that module. Without modulepreload, it finds each nested import one round trip at a time, the same chain of discovery as CSS @import.
modulepreload bundles the whole module graph into one file.
ES modules can't run in the browser without modulepreload.
A regular preload tag can't fetch JavaScript files, only stylesheets and images.

questions.explanation: The browser can only explore an ES module graph one level at a time. It fetches and parses `main.js` before it sees that `main.js` imports `utils.js`, then fetches `utils.js` before it sees its imports, and so on. This is the staircase from earlier in the quiz, in JavaScript instead of CSS. Preloading only the entry module doesn't help much, because the browser still finds everything below it one step at a time. `modulepreload` lists the deeper modules up front, so they download at the same time as the entry module. A plain `preload` can fetch a script, but it treats it as a single file and doesn't help with the rest of the graph.

questions.title: An `` tag has `fetchpriority="high"`. What does that attribute change?

options.text: The priority the browser gives the request after finding it. It doesn't change how early the browser finds it or when the request starts.
The moment the browser finds the image while parsing the HTML.
Whether the browser fetches the image before the user interacts with the page.
The compression level of the image response.

questions.explanation: When the browser finds a request and how urgently it handles it are two separate things, and `fetchpriority` only affects the second. An image deep in the DOM or added late by JavaScript won't be found any sooner because you marked it high. Use `preload` for that. What changes is scheduling. Once the browser knows about the request, a high-priority image gets more of the bandwidth than other requests in progress. That matters for an LCP image, which the browser would otherwise treat like any other image.

questions.title: Which of these uses of resource hints hurt performance?

options.text: Preloading a font the page never uses. It downloads at high priority and delays resources the page actually needs.
Adding preconnect for eight third-party origins on one page, which splits a small early connection budget eight ways instead of spending it where it matters.
Using preload with an as value that doesn't match how the resource is requested later. The browser can't match the preload to the real request, so it downloads the file twice.
Using preconnect for the one origin that serves the page's LCP image.

questions.explanation: Every hint costs something: bandwidth, a connection or priority. Each of these mistakes spends it in the wrong place. A preloaded font the page doesn't use is pure waste and takes bandwidth from what the page actually shows. Preconnecting to eight origins splits a budget that browsers keep small on purpose, mostly on connections that won't help. And the browser matches preloaded responses partly by `as`, so with a wrong or missing value it doesn't recognize its own preload when the real request comes, and downloads the file again. Preconnecting to the one origin that serves your LCP image is targeted and predictable, so it's worth doing.

questions.title: HTTP/2 multiplexes many requests over one connection. What problem does multiplexing NOT solve?

options.text: Limited bandwidth. All the streams share one connection with a fixed speed, so heavy traffic still slows everything down together.
The HTTP/1.1 limit of six connections per origin.
Head-of-line blocking in the HTTP/1.1 request queue on a single connection.
Opening a new connection for every request.

questions.explanation: Multiplexing removes a limit on connections. It doesn't add bandwidth. The two are easy to confuse because both look like "this is taking too long". HTTP/2 removes the six-connection limit, and it removes the HTTP/1.1 head-of-line blocking where one slow response holds up everything behind it on the same connection. It doesn't change how many bytes per second the network can carry. If you request more data than the connection can deliver, everything arrives a little slower together, instead of a few files arriving fast while the rest wait in a visible queue.

questions.title: Where does head-of-line (HOL) blocking happen in each of these?

options.text: HTTP/1.1 without pipelining: at the connection level. A slow response blocks every request waiting behind it on that connection.
HTTP/2 over TCP: at the transport layer. TCP delivers data in order, so one lost packet stalls every stream on the connection until it's resent, even if the streams are unrelated.
HTTP/3 over QUIC: nowhere. QUIC removed head-of-line blocking completely.
HTTP/2 over TCP: nowhere. HTTP/2 multiplexing works independently of TCP.

questions.explanation: Each new protocol version moves head-of-line blocking one layer down. In HTTP/1.1 it happens at the application level. Each connection handles one request at a time, so a slow response holds up everything behind it. HTTP/2 fixes that with multiplexing, but TCP underneath delivers data strictly in order, so one lost packet stalls every stream on the connection until the retransmission arrives. QUIC recovers lost packets separately for each stream over UDP, so a lost packet stalls only its own stream. Head-of-line blocking still isn't completely gone. Data that depends on order within a single stream can still block at the application level.

questions.title: Domain sharding, spreading assets across asset1.example.com, asset2.example.com and so on, made pages faster under HTTP/1.1. Why does it usually make them slower under HTTP/2?

options.text: HTTP/2 already sends as many requests as needed over one connection per origin. Sharding forces extra connections, each with its own handshake, and HTTP/2 can't prioritize requests across separate connections.
HTTP/2 doesn't support multiple domains on one page.
Domain sharding never helped, even under HTTP/1.1.
HTTP/2 needs exactly six domains to work correctly.

questions.explanation: Sharding worked around a real limit. Extra subdomains let the browser open more parallel connections than the six-per-origin limit allowed. HTTP/2 removes that limit, because one connection can carry as many streams as needed, so sharding only adds cost. Each extra origin needs its own DNS lookup, TCP handshake and TLS handshake. It also splits requests across connections that can't be prioritized against each other, which streams on one connection can. When moving to HTTP/2, teams usually combine origins again and undo the sharding.

questions.title: HTTP/2 Server Push let a server send resources before the browser asked for them. Most browsers have now removed it. What replaced it?

options.text: 103 Early Hints, an informational response sent before the final one. It lists resources to preload or preconnect, so the browser can start early without the server forcing bytes on it that it might not need.
The same push mechanism, carried over unchanged into HTTP/3.
Nothing. There's no longer a way to hint resources before the final response headers arrive.
Service workers, which now push resources from the server to the client.

questions.explanation: Server Push was hard to use well. Servers pushed resources the browser already had in its cache, which wasted bandwidth, and they had no reliable way to know what the client needed. 103 Early Hints solves the same problem, starting important downloads before the final response is ready, without that waste. While the server is still preparing the real response, it sends a 103 response with `Link` headers that carry the same hints you'd put in the HTML, such as `preload` and `preconnect`. The browser acts on them right away, often saving a round trip, and it still decides what to fetch.

questions.title: Which statements about an HTTP/2 waterfall with many requests over one connection are true?

options.text: Only the first request on the connection pays for DNS, the TCP handshake and the TLS handshake.
If the requests need more data than the connection's bandwidth can carry, adding more parallel streams won't make them all finish sooner.
Because there's no longer a connection limit per origin, bandwidth is no longer a bottleneck.
Every request still waits behind a six-connection limit, just like in HTTP/1.1.

questions.explanation: One shared connection saves setup time, and it adds no bandwidth. DNS, TCP and TLS happen once, on the first request, and every later stream reuses the open connection. Multiplexing controls how many requests can be in progress, not how many bytes per second the network can carry, so a page limited by bandwidth stays limited however many streams it opens. The six-connection queue is HTTP/1.1 behavior, and it doesn't apply to streams on a shared HTTP/2 connection.
